title: Seafood Pad Thai-Style Noodles with Shrimp, Calamari, Tofu & Cashews
dek: Glossy tamarind rice noodles carry quick-cooked shrimp and calamari, golden tofu, tender egg, crisp bean sprouts, chives, roasted cashews, and plenty of lime.
image_alt: Pad Thai-style rice noodles with shrimp, calamari, golden tofu, egg, bean sprouts, green chives, roasted cashews, and a lime wedge on a white plate
ingredients: 8 oz dried flat rice noodles, about 1/4 inch wide
3 tbsp prepared tamarind paste (not concentrated tamarind extract)
10 oz large raw shrimp, peeled and deveined
6 oz cleaned calamari tubes, sliced into 1/2-inch rings, plus tentacles if included
8 oz extra-firm tofu, pressed dry and cut into 3/4-inch cubes
1 cup garlic chives cut into 2-inch lengths, or 4 scallions cut into 2-inch pieces

instructions.name: Soak the rice noodles
instructions.text: Put the noodles in a large heatproof bowl and cover with very hot tap water. Soak for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring twice, until flexible but still distinctly firm in the center. Drain thoroughly; they finish cooking in the sauce.

instructions.name: Balance the tamarind sauce
instructions.text: Whisk the tamarind paste, fish sauce, brown sugar, lime juice, and red pepper flakes in a small bowl until the sugar mostly dissolves. Taste a drop: it should be boldly sweet, sour, and salty because the noodles will dilute it.

instructions.name: Dry and season the seafood
instructions.text: Pat the shrimp and calamari very dry and season with the kosher salt. Keep them on separate sides of a plate so the calamari can be removed first if it cooks faster. Press the tofu between clean towels until its surface is dry. Wet seafood or tofu steams instead of searing and releases water into the noodles.

instructions.name: Brown the tofu
instructions.text: Heat a 12-inch wok or wide skillet over medium-high heat. Add 1 tablespoon oil and the tofu in one layer. Cook for 4 to 5 minutes, turning two or three times, until golden on several sides. Transfer to a clean plate; browning it separately preserves the crisp edges visible in the finished noodles.

instructions.name: Quick-sear to safe doneness
instructions.text: Increase the heat to high until a drop of water evaporates immediately. Add 1 tablespoon oil, then the shrimp and calamari in one uncrowded layer. Cook, tossing, for 60 to 90 seconds; remove the calamari as soon as opaque and curled. Continue cooking the shrimp just until pink, opaque, and 145°F in the thickest pieces, about 1 minute more. Transfer all seafood to the plate with the tofu.

instructions.name: Set the eggs and aromatics
instructions.text: Reduce the heat to medium-high and add 1 tablespoon oil. Pour in the eggs and leave undisturbed for 20 seconds, then fold into soft curds until they reach 160°F, about 45 seconds total. Push the egg to one side, add the remaining 1 tablespoon oil, shallot, and garlic, and stir-fry for 45 seconds.

instructions.name: Sauce the noodles
instructions.text: Add the drained noodles and tamarind sauce. Toss continuously for 2 to 4 minutes, lifting and turning rather than mashing, until the noodles are tender with a slight chew and have absorbed the glossy sauce. Add 1 tablespoon water at a time only if the pan dries before the noodles soften.

instructions.name: Finish with crunch
instructions.text: Return the seafood, tofu, and any juices. Add 1 1/2 cups bean sprouts, the chives, and 1/3 cup cashews; toss over high heat for 30 to 45 seconds, just until everything is hot. Divide among four plates and finish with the remaining raw sprouts, cashews, and lime wedges. Serve immediately.

why_it_works: Soaking rather than boiling leaves the rice noodles firm enough to absorb the sauce without becoming gummy.
Browning the tofu separately gives it crisp edges, while quick-searing and promptly removing the seafood prevents calamari from turning rubbery as the noodles finish.
Adding some bean sprouts and cashews in the pan and reserving the rest for the top creates both seasoned flavor and fresh crunch.
swaps: Use 1 lb shrimp and omit the calamari; cook the shrimp in two batches if your pan is smaller than 12 inches.
Replace cashews with roasted peanuts for a more familiar Pad Thai finish, or use toasted sunflower seeds for a nut-free version.
For a vegetarian version, omit the seafood, use 1 lb pressed extra-firm tofu total, and replace fish sauce with vegetarian fish-sauce alternative or 2 tbsp soy sauce plus 1 tbsp water.
storage: Cool leftovers promptly and refrigerate in a shallow airtight container for up to 2 days. Reheat in a wide skillet over medium heat with 1 to 2 tablespoons water, tossing until the seafood and noodles reach 165°F. Freezing is not recommended because rice noodles become brittle and reheated calamari toughens.
notes: Prepared tamarind paste varies in strength. Do not substitute highly concentrated tamarind extract one-for-one; dilute it according to its label before measuring.
Have every ingredient measured before heating the pan. Once the seafood goes in, the recipe moves too quickly for stopping to chop.
The calorie and cost estimates include the tofu, cashews, and seafood but not additional restaurant-style garnishes or drinks.

faqs.q: Why are my rice noodles clumping or breaking?
faqs.a: They were probably oversoaked or left drained too long. Soak only until flexible with a firm core, drain immediately before cooking, and toss with lifting motions rather than chopping through them with a spoon.

faqs.q: How do I keep calamari tender?
faqs.a: Calamari is tender when cooked very briefly or braised for a long time; the middle ground is chewy. Slice it evenly, use a properly hot pan, and remove it as soon as the rings turn opaque and curl, usually within 90 seconds.

faqs.q: Can I make this without a wok?
faqs.a: Yes. Use the widest 12-inch skillet you own and cook the seafood in two batches if necessary. A broad surface matters more than the pan's shape because trapped steam prevents browning.

title: Spanish-Style Tomato Butter Beans with Smoked Paprika
dek: Plump butter beans simmer in a glossy garlic-tomato sauce seasoned with smoked paprika, bay, and sherry vinegar for a satisfying pantry skillet.
image_alt: Large white butter beans in a glossy red tomato sauce served in a white bowl
ingredients: 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
2 cans (15 oz each) butter beans or large lima beans, drained and rinsed
2 tsp sherry vinegar, plus more to taste
4 thick slices crusty bread, toasted, for serving

instructions.name: Soften the onion slowly
instructions.text: Heat 2 tablespoons olive oil in a 12-inch skillet over medium heat. Add the onion and 1/2 teaspoon salt. Cook for 7 to 8 minutes, stirring often, until translucent and very soft but not dark; this gives the short sauce a naturally sweet base.

instructions.name: Fry the tomato and spices
instructions.text: Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds. Stir in the tomato paste, smoked paprika, and red pepper flakes. Cook for 60 to 90 seconds, stirring constantly, until the paste darkens to brick red and the paprika smells fragrant. Do not let the garlic or paprika scorch.

instructions.name: Reduce the tomato base
instructions.text: Pour in the crushed tomatoes and broth, scraping up the seasoned film from the skillet. Add the bay leaf, bring to a lively simmer, then reduce the heat to medium-low. Cook uncovered for 8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens enough to leave a trail behind a spoon.

instructions.name: Warm the beans without breaking them
instructions.text: Fold in the butter beans gently. Simmer uncovered for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring by shaking and folding rather than mashing, until the centers are steaming hot and the sauce coats each bean. Add 1 to 2 tablespoons water if the sauce becomes pasty before the beans are hot.

instructions.name: Brighten and serve
instructions.text: Remove the bay leaf. Stir in the sherry vinegar, black pepper, and remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil. Taste and adjust salt or vinegar. Spoon the glossy beans into shallow bowls and serve with toasted bread for dragging through the tomato sauce.

why_it_works: Cooking tomato paste and paprika in oil concentrates the tomato and disperses the pepper's smoky aroma through the entire sauce.
Large canned butter beans need only a gentle simmer; folding them into an already-reduced sauce keeps them whole instead of chalky or broken.
Sherry vinegar added after cooking restores brightness that long-simmered tomato can lose, while a final spoonful of olive oil makes the sauce look and taste glossy.
swaps: Use cannellini beans if butter beans are unavailable; begin checking after 5 minutes because smaller beans heat more quickly.
Red wine vinegar can replace sherry vinegar, though its flavor is sharper, so start with 1 teaspoon and taste.
For a non-vegetarian variation, brown 4 oz diced Spanish-style chorizo first, remove it, and return it with the beans; reduce the added salt and olive oil.
storage: Cool within 2 hours and refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 4 days. Reheat gently in a covered skillet with a splash of water until bubbling and 165°F, folding only once or twice. Freeze without the bread for up to 2 months; thaw overnight and refresh with a few drops of sherry vinegar after reheating.
notes: Sweet smoked paprika supplies smoke without making the dish hot. Use hot smoked paprika only if you want a noticeably spicy sauce.
Rinsing canned beans removes excess packing liquid and sodium, but drain them well so the tomato sauce does not become watery.
The calorie estimate includes one slice of toast per serving; the beans alone are approximately 255 calories per serving.

faqs.q: Are butter beans and lima beans the same thing?
faqs.a: Butter bean is a common name for mature lima beans. Canned products labeled either butter beans or large lima beans work here; choose the largest, creamiest-looking beans available.

Yes. Cook about 1 1/4 cups dried large lima beans separately until completely tender, then measure 3 cups drained cooked beans for the recipe. Acidic tomato sauce can delay softening, so do not cook dried beans from raw in the sauce.

faqs.q: Why did my beans fall apart?
faqs.a: They were either very soft from the can or stirred too aggressively. Drain gently, add them only after the sauce reduces, keep the simmer modest, and fold with a silicone spatula instead of stirring in circles.

title: One-Bowl Carrot Snacking Cake with Tangy Cream Cheese Frosting
dek: A deeply spiced, single-layer carrot cake stays plush with oil and yogurt, then gets a thick sweep of lemony cream cheese frosting and cheerful orange sprinkles.
image_alt: Round single-layer carrot cake with thick white cream cheese frosting and orange sprinkles, with several slices cut on a white platter
ingredients: 3/4 cup (150 g) packed light brown sugar
1/3 cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt, at room temperature
2 cups (200 g) finely grated peeled carrots
8 oz full-fat block cream cheese, softened but still cool

instructions.name: Prepare the pan and oven
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 350°F with a rack in the center. Grease a 9-inch round light-colored metal cake pan, line the bottom with parchment, and grease the parchment. Set the pan on a sheet of foil only if it has a removable bottom.

instructions.name: Whisk the dry ingredients
instructions.text: In a large bowl, whisk the flour, baking powder, baking soda, cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg, and salt for 30 seconds. Break up any brown-sugar lumps separately with your fingertips before adding wet ingredients.

instructions.name: Build the one-bowl batter
instructions.text: Make a wide well in the dry ingredients. Add the brown sugar, granulated sugar, eggs, oil, yogurt, and 1 teaspoon vanilla to the well. Whisk the wet center until smooth, then switch to a flexible spatula and fold outward just until a few dry streaks remain. Fold in the grated carrots until evenly distributed; do not beat the batter smooth.

instructions.name: Bake to a set center
instructions.text: Scrape the batter into the prepared pan and level the top. Bake for 36 to 44 minutes, rotating once after 28 minutes, until the cake springs back lightly, a tester has a few moist crumbs but no wet batter, and the center registers 200°F to 205°F.

instructions.name: Cool completely
instructions.text: Cool the cake in its pan on a rack for 15 minutes. Run a thin knife around the edge, invert onto the rack, remove the parchment, and turn right-side up. Cool for at least 45 minutes more. The frosting will melt and slide if the cake is even slightly warm; the listed cook time includes this cooling period.

instructions.name: Make the tangy frosting
instructions.text: Beat the cream cheese and butter with a hand mixer on medium-low just until smooth, about 45 seconds. Add the confectioners' sugar in three additions on low speed. Beat in the lemon zest, lemon juice, 1/2 teaspoon vanilla, and pinch of salt just until fluffy, 30 to 45 seconds; overbeating can loosen cream cheese frosting.

instructions.name: Frost and decorate
instructions.text: Place the completely cool cake on a platter. Spread the frosting over the top in a thick, even layer, leaving the sides bare. Scatter the orange jimmies over the frosting, chill for 20 minutes for neat slices, and cut with a hot, dry knife.

why_it_works: Oil remains fluid when cool, and yogurt adds moisture plus enough acidity to support the baking soda, keeping the single layer plush for days.
Finely grated carrots soften within the cake and distribute moisture more evenly than coarse shreds.
Cool cream cheese and restrained mixing create a frosting thick enough to hold the generous swoops and sprinkles shown on the finished cake.
swaps: Replace Greek yogurt with an equal weight of full-fat sour cream.
Fold 1/2 cup toasted chopped walnuts or drained crushed pineapple into the batter, but expect the finished cake to differ from the smooth, nut-free version pictured.
For cupcakes, divide the batter among 12 lined standard wells and bake at 350°F for 18 to 23 minutes; cool completely before frosting.
storage: Because of the cream cheese frosting, refrigerate the covered cake within 2 hours and keep it chilled for up to 5 days. Let slices stand at room temperature for 20 to 30 minutes before serving, or microwave an unfrosted slice for 8 seconds. Freeze unfrosted cake tightly wrapped for up to 2 months; thaw overnight in the refrigerator and frost after thawing.
notes: Weigh the flour and carrots when possible. Packed flour dries the crumb, while too much carrot can make the center gummy.
Use block cream cheese rather than whipped tub-style spread, which contains more air and water and produces loose frosting.
Jimmies stay tidy on soft frosting better than nonpareils, whose color may bleed after refrigeration.

faqs.q: Can I grate the carrots in a food processor?
faqs.a: Yes, use the fine shredding disk and weigh 200 g after peeling. If your processor makes long strands, pulse them two or three times with the blade so slices do not pull out strings of carrot.

faqs.q: Why did my carrot cake sink in the middle?
faqs.a: The center was likely underbaked, the leaveners were old, or the batter was overmixed. Verify 200°F to 205°F in the center, test baking soda and powder for freshness, and fold only until the flour disappears.

faqs.q: Can I make the cake ahead?
faqs.a: Bake the layer up to 2 days ahead, cool completely, and wrap it tightly at room temperature. Make the frosting up to 3 days ahead and refrigerate; let it soften for 15 minutes and stir briefly before frosting.
